The '''''Act respecting the laicity of the State''''' ({{Langx|fr|Loi sur la laïcité de l'État}}), introduced and commonly referred to as '''Bill 21''' or '''Law 21''' ({{Langx|fr|Loi 21}}), is a statute passed by the [[National Assembly of Quebec]] in 2019 which asserts that [[Quebec]] is a [[Secular state|lay state]] (secular state). It prohibits the wearing of religious symbols by certain public employees in positions of authority and those who were already in office when the bill was introduced. The statute operates despite the [[Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms|Quebec ''Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms'']],<ref name="Act">{{Cite canlaw|short title=Act respecting the laicity of the State|abbr=SQ|year=2019|chapter=12|section=1.|link=https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/L-0.3}}</ref>{{rp|s. 33}} and also [[section 33|notwithstanding]] certain sections of the ''[[Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms]]''.<ref name=Act/>{{rp|s. 34}}

On April 20, 2021, the [[Superior Court of Quebec]] upheld most of the law, despite stating that the law violates the [[freedom of expression]] and [[freedom of religion|religion]] of religious minorities (especially [[Islam in Canada|Muslim]] women),<ref name=cbc1>{{cite news|title=Quebec Superior Court upholds most of religious symbols ban, but English-language schools exempt|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/bill-21-religious-symbols-ban-quebec-court-ruling-1.5993431|publisher=[[CBC News]]|date=2021-04-21}}</ref><ref name="Global News">{{cite news|title=Quebec's top court begins hearing appeals on secularism law known as Bill 21|url=https://globalnews.ca/news/9257556/quebec-bill-21-appeal-court/|publisher=[[Global News]]}}</ref> because the National Assembly invoked the notwithstanding clause. However, the court did rule that the law was inoperative with respect to [[Anglo-Quebecer|English-language]] school boards and members of the [[National Assembly of Quebec|National Assembly]] as it infringed on their constitutional rights,<ref>{{cite web |work=CTV News |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/montreal/article/court-mostly-upholds-controversial-quebec-secularism-law-exempts-english-school-boards/ |title=Court mostly upholds controversial Quebec secularism law, exempts English school boards |author=Selena Ross |date=2021-04-20 |access-date=2022-02-02 }}</ref><ref>[https://www.canlii.org/fr/qc/qccs/doc/2021/2021qccs1466/2021qccs1466.html ''Hak c. Procureur général du Québec'', 2021 QCCS 1466 (CanLII), paras. 1129–1131, 1138–1140.]</ref> which argues that [[Language rights|minority language rights]] cannot be overridden by the notwithstanding clause.<ref name=cbc1/> The Government of Quebec appealed the judgment to the [[Quebec Court of Appeal]].<ref>{{cite web |language=fr-ca |title=Les commissions scolaires anglophones exemptées de la Loi sur la laïcité de l'État |url=https://ici.radio-canada.ca/nouvelle/1786293/cour-superieure-validite-loi-laicite-etat |editor=Radio-Canada |date=2021-04-20}}</ref> The [[Fédération autonome de l'enseignement|Autonomous Federation of Education]] also decided to bring the case to the higher court.<ref>{{cite web |author=La Presse canadienne |title=Loi sur la laïcité de l'État : la FAE en appellera du jugement de la Cour supérieure |url=https://ici.radio-canada.ca/nouvelle/1787519/projet-loi-21-quebec-contestation-judiciaire-cour-superieure-appel |editor=Radio-Canada|date=2021-04-24}}</ref> English-language school boards must apply the statute until the appeal is decided; an interlocutory application to temporarily exempt the school boards from it was rejected by the Quebec Court of Appeal in November 2021.<ref>{{cite news |newspaper=Montreal Gazette |url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/emsb-loses-bid-to-temporarily-suspend-bill-21 |date=2021-11-10 |accessdate=2022-02-02 |author=Jason Magder |title=EMSB loses bid to temporarily suspend Quebec's religious symbols law }}</ref>

While the statute is supported by most of Quebec's population, some argue that it does not go far enough and should extend to daycares, while others argue that the statute is [[discriminatory]] against [[Religion in Quebec|religious groups like Muslims, Jews, and Sikhs]]. Disapproval of the statute is more widespread in [[English Canada]] than in [[French Canada]].

== Contents and passage ==
The conservative, nationalist party [[Coalition Avenir Québec]] (CAQ) had campaigned for a law related to laicity during the [[2018 Quebec general election|2018 provincial election]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Law n°21 : An Act respecting the laicity of the State - National Assembly of Québec|url=https://www.assnat.qc.ca/en/travaux-parlementaires/projets-loi/projet-loi-21-42-1.html|access-date=April 5, 2019|website=www.assnat.qc.ca|language=en}}</ref> After the CAQ gained a majority in the [[National Assembly of Quebec]], it introduced Bill 21 on March 28, 2019. As enacted, the law bans public workers in positions of "authority" from wearing religious symbols, specifically while they are on duty. According to the text of the bill, the laicity of the state is defined by a neutral religious stance, keeping state and religious affairs apart, as well as promoting equality and freedom of conscience and religion among citizens.<ref name=Act/>

The first section of ''An Act Respecting laicity of the State'' asserts that Quebec is a "lay State". The laicity of the state is based on four principles:
* the [[Equality of all citizens before the law|equality of all citizens]]
*the [[Separation of state and religion|separation of State and religions]]
*the [[Laicity|religious neutrality of the State]]
*[[freedom of conscience]] and [[freedom of religion]]

According to the second paragraph of section 4, "State laicity also requires that all persons have the right to lay [[Quebec Legislature|parliamentary]], [[Government of Quebec|government]] and [[Judiciary of Canada|judicial institutions]], and to lay public services".<ref name=Act/>

Immigration Minister [[Simon Jolin-Barrette]] said all religious symbols, regardless of the size of the object, would be prohibited, but not religious tattoos or hairstyles such as Rastafarian [[dreadlocks]]. The law affects:

* Any public employee who carries a weapon, including police officers, courthouse constables, bodyguards, prison guards, and wildlife officers
* Crown prosecutors, government lawyers, and judges
* School principals, vice principals, and teachers

A [[grandfather clause]] exempts some public workers as long as they continue to hold the same job, at the same institution. The law also outlines rules that require people to uncover their faces to receive a public service for identification or security purposes, such as taking public transit with a reduced-fare photo ID card. However, people who have their faces covered for medical reasons or for job-related requirements are exempt from these rules.<ref name = Act/>

The law applies when receiving government services, including:

* Municipal services such as public transit
* Doctors, dentists, and midwives in public institutions
* Subsidised daycares
* School boards<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|title=What's in Quebec's secularism bill: Religious symbols, uncovered faces and a charter workaround {{pipe}} CBC News|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/quebec-laicity-secularism-bill-1.5075547}}</ref>

The Act also invokes [[Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms|section 33 of the ''Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms'']], the notwithstanding clause, and states that the Act shall have effect notwithstanding [[Section 2 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms|section 2 of the Canadian Charter]] (which protects freedom of religion and freedom of expression), and sections 7 to 15 of the Canadian Charter ([[Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms|section 15 of the Canadian Charter]] prohibits discrimination by governments, including on the basis of religion).<ref name=Act/>{{rp|s. 34}} The Act also states that it will apply despite sections 1 to 38 of the Quebec ''Charter of human rights and freedoms''.<ref name=Act/>{{rp|s. 33}} These provisions were included to avoid legal challenges based on the ''Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms'' and the ''Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms'', which was amended to assert that "state laicity" is of "fundamental importance".<ref name="auto" /><ref>{{Cite news|title=Quebec's bill to ban religious symbols sparks condemnation in the province and Ottawa|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-quebec-tables-legislation-on-religious-symbols-ban-includes/|newspaper=The Globe and Mail|date=March 28, 2019 |last1=Perreaux |first1=Les }}</ref><ref name="auto1">{{Cite web|title=Quebec government's proposed secularism law would ban public workers from wearing religious symbols {{pipe}} CBC News|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/quebec-notwithstanding-religious-symbols-1.5073945}}</ref>

[[François Legault]] initially supported keeping the [[crucifix]] that has been in the Legislative Assembly chamber since 1936, arguing the legislature's crucifix was a symbol of "heritage and history" rather than a religious icon<ref>[https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/quebec-francois-legault-crucifix-religious-symbols-1.4858757]</ref><ref>[https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-45842471]</ref><ref>[https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-news/crucifix-will-stay-in-quebecs-national-assembly-caq-says/]</ref> and polls showing that over 55% of Quebecers supported the [[crucifix]] remaining.<ref>[https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-news/majority-of-quebecers-support-the-caqs-plan-to-ban-religious-symbols/]</ref><ref>[https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/public-religious-symbols-quebec-poll-1.4919997]</ref> The crucifix was eventually removed.<ref>[https://www.ctvnews.ca/montreal/article/national-assembly-votes-to-remove-crucifix/]</ref>

It passed on June 16, 2019 by a 73–35 vote, with the backing of the CAQ and the [[Parti Québécois]] (PQ). The [[Quebec Liberal Party]] and [[Québec solidaire]] were opposed. The CAQ government also introduced last-minute amendments toughening the law, making provisions for a minister to verify that it is being obeyed and to demand corrective measures if necessary.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Quebec passes bill banning public servants from wearing religious symbols|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-quebec-legislature-expected-to-pass-bill-21-late-sunday/|newspaper=The Globe and Mail|date=June 16, 2019 |last1=Perreaux |first1=Les }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Quebec bans religious symbols for state workers in new law|url=https://globalnews.ca/news/5397857/quebec-religious-symbol-ban-passed/|website=Global News}}</ref>
===2024 Renewal===
On May 2, 2024, the National Assembly of Quebec voted to renew Bill 21 by using the [[notwithstanding clause]] for five more years until 2029. The assembly vote was 83 for and 26 opposed. The CAQ and PQ parties voted for the bill, while the Quebec Liberal Party and Québec solidaire voted against it.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Authier |first=Philip |date=2 May 2024 |title=Legault calls out Liberals, QS for voting against renewal of notwithstanding clause |url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/politics/legault-calls-out-liberals-qs-for-voting-against-renewal-of-notwithstanding-clause |work=The Gazette}}</ref>

===Bill 94 (2025)===
{{empty section|date=December 2025}}

===Bill 9 (2025)===
{{empty section|date=December 2025}}
On November 27, 2025, the Coalition Avenir Québec party tabled Bill 9 that would strengthen Bill 21 passed in 2019.<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 27, 2025|title=Quebec's new secularism bill targets daycare workers, prayer spaces and religious meals
|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/quebec-secularism-bill-9.6993278 |access-date=November 27, 2025 |work=}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=November 27, 2025|title=Update: Quebec's sweeping new secularism bill targets public prayer, but Christmas parties are OK
|url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-plans-to-ban-street-prayers-as-it-moves-to-beef-up-secularism-law |access-date=November 27, 2025 |work=}}</ref>

On April 2 2026, The [[National Assembly of Quebec|National Assembly in Quebec]] passed Bill 9 that expands on its secularism law [[Bill 21]]. It bans wearing religious symbols for daycare workers and prayer spaces in public institutions. CAQ and Parti Québécois, voted in favour of the legislation, while the Liberals and Québec Solidaire voted against it.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/quebec-secularism-bill-9.7151637| title=Quebec passes expanded secularism law targeting daycare workers, public prayer| date=April 2, 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/montreal/article/quebec-passes-law-banning-street-prayers-prayer-rooms-in-universities-cegeps/|title=Quebec passes law banning street prayers, prayer rooms in universities, CEGEPs| date=April 2, 2026 }}</ref>

==Prior legislation==

=== Proposed Charter of Values (2013)===
The Parti Québécois in 2013 under Premier [[Pauline Marois]] proposed the [[Quebec Charter of Values]], a law banning the display of "ostentatious" religious symbols, but they were unable to pass it before losing an election some months thereafter.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Québec Values Charter {{!}} The Canadian Encyclopedia|url=https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/the-charter-of-quebec-values|access-date=2021-12-16|website=www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca}}</ref>

===Bill 62 (2017)===
''An act to foster adherence to State religious neutrality and, in particular, to provide a framework for requests for accommodations on religious grounds in certain bodies'',<ref name="veconomist" /> introduced as Bill 62 and passed by Premier [[Philippe Couillard]]'s [[Quebec Liberal Party|Liberal]] government in October 2017 made world headlines.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/quebec-face-covering-bill-62-1.4364055|title=How Quebec's face-covering ban stacks up to laws elsewhere around the globe}}</ref><ref name="veconomist" /> The law banned a person whose face is covered from delivering or receiving a public service.<ref name="veconomist">{{cite news|author=M.D.|title=Quebec's ban on face-coverings risks inflaming inter-communal tensions|url=https://www.economist.com/blogs/erasmus/2017/10/quebec-islam-and-face-covering|newspaper=[[The Economist]]|date=October 20, 2017 |access-date=March 12, 2020}}</ref> Justice Minister [[Stéphanie Vallée]] stated that people could seek religious exemption on a "case by case" basis.<ref>{{cite news|last=Boissinot|first=Jacques|title=How will Quebec's Bill 62 work? What we know (and don't) so far|work=[[The Globe and Mail]]|date=24 October 2017|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/national/quebec-bill-62-explainer/article36700916/|access-date=13 August 2018}}</ref>

==== Criticism ====
The ban has worried some Muslims who consider [[Niqāb|female veiling]] a necessary part of their religion,<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/national/quebec-bans-face-covering-in-public-services-raising-worries-among-muslims/article36638544/|title=Quebec bans face covering in public services, raising worries among Muslims|newspaper=The Globe and Mail|date=October 18, 2017|last1=Peritz|first1=Ingrid}}</ref> defining the move as [[Islamophobia in Canada|Islamophobia]].<ref name="ec">{{cite news|title=Wanting to ban the veil, Quebec bans sunglasses, too|url=https://www.economist.com/news/americas/21731687-fooling-none-quebeckers-none-time-wanting-ban-veil-quebec-bans|access-date=November 24, 2017|newspaper=[[The Economist]]|date=November 24, 2017}}</ref> The ban also worried Sikh men, who would be unable to wear their religious headgear. There were calls for criticism, arguing that the bill unfairly targets specific religions rather than all of them. This argument arises because some religious garments are easier to remove or hide under regular clothing such as crosses used in Christianity compared to turbans, hijabs, and burqas.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Baum |first=Gregory |date=1986 |title=Catholicism and Secularization in Quebec |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24459103 |journal=CrossCurrents |volume=36 |issue=4 |pages=436–458 |jstor=24459103 |issn=0011-1953}}</ref> Prime Minister [[Justin Trudeau]] spoke out against it.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2017/oct/20/justin-trudeau-quebec-burqa-ban-niqab-new-law|title=Trudeau on Quebec face-cover ban: not our business to tell women what to wear|first=Ashifa|last=Kassam|newspaper=The Guardian |date=October 20, 2017|via=www.theguardian.com}}</ref> Several scholars have also criticised the ban.<ref name="veconomist" /> The ban was challenged by the [[Canadian Civil Liberties Association]] and the [[National Council of Canadian Muslims]] in the [[Quebec Superior Court]].<ref name="ec" /> Meanwhile, the [[Parti Québécois]] (PQ) and the [[Coalition Avenir Québec]] (CAQ) argued the ban was not extensive enough.<ref name="veconomist" /> Some journalists accused Couillard of supporting the ban for "perceived political advantage",<ref name="veconomist" /> while a majority of the general public expressed their support for this move.<ref>{{cite web| url = https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/bill-62-support-in-quebec-1.4366032| title = For supporters, Quebec's face-covering law a matter of safety and respect {{!}} CBC News}}</ref>

==== Public opinion ====
With regard to public opinion, a 2017 [[Ipsos]] poll found that 76 percent of Quebecers backed Bill 62, with 24 percent opposing it. The same survey found that 68 percent of Canadians, in general, supported a law similar to Bill 62 in their part of Canada.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Abedi|first1=Maham|title=68% of Canadians want Quebec's face-coverings ban in their province|url=https://globalnews.ca/video/3828903/new-ipsos-poll-reveals-cross-canada-sentiment-about-quebecs-bill-62-face-veil-ban|website=[[Global News]]|access-date=October 28, 2017|date=October 27, 2017}}</ref> A 2017 [[Angus Reid (market research)|Angus Reid Institute]] poll found that 70 percent of Canadians outside of Quebec supported "legislation similar to Bill 62" where they lived in the country, with 30 percent opposing it.<ref>{{cite news|title=Four-in-ten outside Quebec would prohibit women wearing niqabs from receiving government services|url=https://angusreid.org/bill-62-face-covering/|website=[[Angus Reid (market research)|Angus Reid]]|access-date=October 28, 2017|date=October 27, 2017|last1=Korzinski |first1=David }}</ref>

==== Court challenges ====
Several legal challenges were filed against the law and a judge ruled that the face-covering ban cannot be applicable while analyzed by another court, because of the irreversible injury it may cause some women of the Muslim faith. Another judge granted an injunction on that section questioned in court by the [[National Council of Canadian Muslims]] with the participation of the [[Canadian Civil Liberties Association]]. In the judgment of the court, said section contravenes the freedoms guaranteed by the ''[[Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms]]'', and the ''[[Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms]]''.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/quebec-judge-once-again-suspends-application-of-provinces-face-covering-law|title=Quebec's face-covering law suspended for second time, with judge citing rights concerns|newspaper=National Post|date=June 29, 2018|last1=Valiante|first1=Giuseppe}}</ref>

The Quebec Liberal Party government confirmed that it would not appeal the suspension of the key article of its ''Religious Neutrality Act''. The [[Government of Quebec]] preferred to wait for a judgement on the substance and constitutionality of the law.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://journalmetro.com/actualites/montreal/1678693/port-de-signes-religieux-des-partis-pourraient-recourir-a-la-clause-derogatoire/|title=Port de signes religieux: des partis pourraient recourir à la clause dérogatoire|date=August 14, 2018}}</ref>

If the Liberal government had been re-elected in the general election on October 1, 2018, Premier Philippe Couillard said he would be ready to go to the [[Supreme Court of Canada]], if necessary, to defend Bill 62.<ref>{{cite web| url = https://quebec.huffingtonpost.ca/2018/09/10/philippe-couillard-neutralite-religieuse-etat_a_23523125/| url-status = dead| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180911045208/https://quebec.huffingtonpost.ca/2018/09/10/philippe-couillard-neutralite-religieuse-etat_a_23523125/| archive-date = 2018-09-11| title = Philippe Couillard irait jusqu'en Cour suprême pour défendre la neutralité religieuse de l'État}}</ref> From his previous comments on the matter, Couillard was not likely to preserve the face covering the ban by invoking [[Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms|section 33 of the ''Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms'']], the notwithstanding clause.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.thestar.com/opinion/star-columnists/2018/09/12/will-quebec-be-the-next-province-to-use-the-notwithstanding-clause.html|title=Opinion {{pipe}} Will Quebec be the next province to use the 'notwithstanding' clause?|date=September 12, 2018|newspaper=The Toronto Star}}</ref> Couillard stated that his government, in passing Bill 62, did not use the notwithstanding clause by design, asserting that the court would uphold his government's limited ban as reasonable and justified.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ipolitics.ca/2018/09/12/doug-fords-use-of-notwithstanding-clause-music-to-the-ears-of-quebecs-francois-legault/|title=Doug Ford's use of notwithstanding clause music to the ears of Quebec's Francois Legault|work=iPolitics |date=September 12, 2018}}</ref>

==Reception==

=== Government ===
Premier [[François Legault]] said the bill was moderate and that by having a law like this, it would prevent a party like France's [[Marine Le Pen]] [[National Rally]] in Quebec.<ref>{{cite web | title=Bill 21: Legault says the government listened to the majority and acted | work=montrealgazette | url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec/bill-21-legault-says-the-government-listened-to-the-majority-and-acted }}</ref>

=== Opposition ===
The Quebec Liberal Party said the law would go too far, particularly with respect to Muslim women, and continued to advocate a ban only on religious clothing which covered the face, such as the [[niqab]]. Québec solidaire said that it was opposed to any ban on the wearing of religious symbols.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ici.radio-canada.ca/nouvelle/1161518/signes-religieux-quebec-solidaire-vote-aucune-regle |title=Signes religieux : les membres de Québec solidaire votent pour la totale liberté |website=Radio-Canada.ca |date=March 30, 2019 }}</ref> [[2020 Quebec Liberal Party leadership election|Quebec Liberal leadership]] candidate, [[Dominique Anglade]], argued that "We are all in favour of [[secularism]], but not the way it was done with Bill 21."<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/bill-21-would-not-be-shielded-by-notwithstanding-clause-under-anglades-watch|title=No notwithstanding clause for Bill 21 under my watch: Anglade |work=Montreal Gazette|last=Authier|first=Philip |date=November 22, 2019 |access-date=November 24, 2019 }}</ref> The Parti Québécois said the ban did not go far enough, and that it should have been extended to public daycare workers, as in its proposed legislation.<ref name="auto1" />

[[Gérard Bouchard]] and [[Charles Taylor (philosopher)|Charles Taylor]], authors of the [[Bouchard-Taylor Commission|Bouchard-Taylor report]] on reasonable accommodations, raised concern that the law makes the province not look like a "decent society" and will only feed an intolerance toward minorities.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec/gerard-bouchard-challenges-legitimacy-of-bill-21-at-hearings|title=Gérard Bouchard challenges legitimacy of Bill 21 at hearings |work=Montreal Gazette|last=Authier|first=Philip |date=May 9, 2019 |access-date=November 14, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/montreal/article/gerard-bouchard-declares-opposition-to-quebecs-radical-secularism-bill/|title=Gerard Bouchard declares opposition to Quebec's 'radical' secularism bill|date=May 8, 2019|website=Montreal|language=en|access-date=November 14, 2019}}</ref>

Various forms of resistance to Bill 21 have emerged since its inception. Some are the legal challenges described below. The Coalition Inclusion Quebec is taking legal action on the basis that Bill 21 specifically targets Muslim women.<ref name="New court challenge brought against Quebec's secularism law">{{cite web |last1=Montpetit |first1=J |title=New court challenge brought against Quebec's secularism law |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/new-court-challenge-brought-against-quebec-s-secularism-law-1.5299183 |website=CBC |access-date=November 6, 2019}}</ref> The Coalition Inclusion Quebec is challenging the use of the notwithstanding clause because it cannot be used against Section 28 of the Charter, regarding gender discrimination. Another court case is being filed by the [[English Montreal School Board]] on the basis of violating minority language rights.<ref>{{cite news |title=EMSB prepares legal fight over secularism law that chair says "breeds intolerance" |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/english-montreal-school-board-legal-fight-bill-21-secularism-religious-symbols-ban-1.5298586 |access-date=November 6, 2019 |publisher=CBC |date=September 26, 2019}}</ref> [[Calgary City Council]] and [[Edmonton City Council]] voted unanimously to condemn Bill 21 with mayors [[Naheed Nenshi]] of Calgary and [[Don Iveson]] of Edmonton urging other municipal governments to speak out against Bill 21.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://pub-edmonton.escribemeetings.com/Meeting.aspx?Id=057B539C-BCF4-4139-9150-3D06C47C9677&Agenda=PostMinutes#_Toc43833555 |title=CITY COUNCIL MINUTES June 22/23, 2020 – Council Chamber |date=June 22, 2020 |publisher=Edmonton City Council |access-date=March 6, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Bell |first1=D |title="It's terrifying": Naheed Nenshi calls for national groundswell against Quebec secularism bill |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/calgary/nenshi-opposition-quebec-bill-21-1.5305955 |access-date=November 6, 2019 |publisher=CBC |date=October 2, 2019}}</ref>

[[New Democratic Party]] leader [[Jagmeet Singh]] said that he would support federal intervention in court to challenge Bill 21.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-12-14|title=NDP leader would back federal intervention in court challenge to Quebec's Bill 21|url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/montreal/article/ndp-leader-would-back-federal-intervention-in-court-challenge-to-quebecs-bill-21/|access-date=2022-01-05|website=CTV News Montreal|publisher=The Canadian Press|language=en}}</ref>

Federal [[antisemitism]] envoy [[Irwin Cotler]] has called Bill 21 "discriminatory", adding that "It does not so much separate religion and state as it authorizes state interference with religion".<ref>{{Cite news|date=2022-01-04|title=Ottawa's antisemitism envoy Irwin Cotler calls Quebec's Bill 21 discriminatory|language=en-CA|work=The Globe and Mail|publisher=The Canadian Press|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-ottawas-anti-semitism-envoy-irwin-cotler-says-quebecs-secularism-law/|access-date=2022-01-05}}</ref>

William Steinberg compares Bill 21 to "[[Ethnic cleansing|ethnic cleansing]]"<ref>{{Cite news |last=Shingler |first=Benjamin |date=April 5, 2019 |title=Opposition to Quebec's Bill 21 intensifies as minister pleads for calm |work=CBC News |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/quebec-bill-21-opposition-1.5083340}}</ref> as it discriminates against minority religions that have more requirements for religious clothing and headgear.

=== Support ===
Prior to the [[Quiet Revolution]] in the 1960s, Quebec was heavily influenced by the [[Catholic Church]], including the education system. The arrangement was unpopular, with many older Quebeckers later reporting negative experiences while in school. People saw the role of the church as a "necessary step on the road to modernity, to building a secular, more egalitarian society, freed from the evils of superstition". Religion came to be seen as a [[Social constructionism|social construct]] that society and people can choose to adopt or disregard.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Polèse|first=Mario|date=August 4, 2021|title=Quebec's Bill 21: Is there room for more than one view of religion in Canada?|url=https://policyoptions.irpp.org/magazines/august-2021/quebecs-bill-21-is-there-room-for-more-than-one-view-of-religion-in-canada/|access-date=2021-12-16|website=Policy Options|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=2020-11-10|title=Bill 21 supporters testify that religious symbols send wrong message to kids|language=en-CA|work=The Toronto Star|url=https://www.thestar.com/politics/2020/11/10/bill-21-supporters-testify-that-religious-symbols-send-wrong-message-to-kids.html|access-date=2021-12-16|issn=0319-0781}}</ref>

A 2019 poll conducted by [[Forum Research]] reported the law enjoyed 64 per cent support in Quebec.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Majority of Canadians disapprove of Bill 21, but Quebecers are in favour: poll|url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec/majority-of-canadians-disapprove-of-bill-21-but-quebecers-are-in-favour-poll|access-date=2021-12-16|website=montrealgazette|language=en-CA}}</ref>

The Parti Québécois supports it but, said the ban did not go far enough, and that it should have been extended to public daycare workers, as in its proposed legislation.<ref>{{cite web |title=Quebec government's proposed secularism law would ban public workers from wearing religious symbols |date=March 28, 2019 |website=[[CBC News]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230531003048/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/quebec-notwithstanding-religious-symbols-1.5073945 |archive-date=May 31, 2023 |url-status=live |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/quebec-notwithstanding-religious-symbols-1.5073945}}</ref>

[[Mouvement laïque québécois]] supports the Bill, but they say it doesn't go far enough.<ref>{{cite web |title=Hearings on constitutionality of Quebec's secularism law underway in Court of Appeal |date=November 7, 2022 |website=[[CBC News]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230614013109/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/bill-21-appeal-begins-1.6640434 |archive-date=June 14, 2023 |url-status=live |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/bill-21-appeal-begins-1.6640434}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/religious-symbols-which-groups-are-for-or-against-quebecs-bill-21 | title=Religious symbols: Which groups are for or against Quebec's Bill 21? | work=montrealgazette }}</ref>

Several studies show that the Quebec population was more in favour of banning Sikh and Muslim religious symbols. In a survey conducted in December 2018 by Angus Reid, respondents were significantly more in favour of allowing Judeo-Christian religious symbols to wear (between 57% and 42% of support) such as crucifixes and [[kippah]]s and more in favour of banning Sikh and Muslim religious symbols such as the hijab or [[dastar]].<ref>[https://www.ledevoir.com/societe/553869/laicite-l-appui-au-projet-de-loi-21-se-maintient#]</ref> In a poll conducted by Leger, the hijab was perceived positively by only 26% of respondents compared to 55% for the Christian cross. 88% of Quebecers who had a negative view of Islam supported banning teachers from wearing religious symbols.<ref>[https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/a-new-poll-shows-support-for-bill-21-is-built-on-anti-islam-sentiment]</ref><ref>[https://www.ledevoir.com/societe/554660/laicite-les-quebecois-nage-dans-les-contradictions]</ref> For Claire Durand, a sociology professor at the University of Montreal, "This leads to the conclusion that there is no support for the secularism of the state, but rather a resistance to recent diversity."<ref>[http://plus.lapresse.ca/screens/7de4514c-e1fe-4073-9e90-ff84dd83409d__7C___0.html]</ref>

A 2022 study by the Association for Canadian Studies shows that the majority of supporters of Bill 21 have negative views of Islam (75%), Sikhism (66.1%), while a minority of them 36.5% had a negative view of Christianity (36.%) or Judaism (49.0%). With regard to religious symbols, the majority of supporters of Bill 21 had a negative opinion of the hijab (78.1%), the Sikh dastar (75.7%) and the kippah (54.6%). As for the Christian cross, only 38.5% of supporters had a negative opinion of this symbol.<ref>[https://acs-metropolis.ca/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Rapport_Sondage-Loi-21_AEC_Leger-12.pdf]</ref>

=== Federal elections ===
Bill 21 was debated in the [[2019 Canadian federal election|2019 federal election]]. [[Bloc Québécois|Bloc Quebecois]] leader [[Yves-François Blanchet|Yves-Francois Blanchet]] stated this was a provincial matter and not relevant to the federal government's jurisdiction but did campaign in favour of Bill 21.<ref>{{cite news|author=<!-- Global News Staff, no byline-->|date=October 8, 2019|title=Bloc Quebecois leader Blanchet says secularism, Bill 21 shouldn't be campaign issue|publisher=Global News|url=https://globalnews.ca/news/6009175/bloc-quebecois-leader-blanchet-bill-21/|access-date=November 6, 2019}}</ref> When explaining why being called a [[Quebec nationalism|nationalist]] to Canada Press is not seen a pejorative, Joseph Yvon Thériault, a sociology professor at [[Université du Québec à Montréal|University of Quebec at Montreal]], compared Bill 21 to stricter legislation in European countries such as [[Secularism in France|France]] and Belgium as an argument that Quebec nationalism is based on moderation.<ref>{{Cite news|title=In Quebec, being a nationalist is a positive, not a negative|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-in-quebec-being-a-nationalist-is-a-positive-not-a-negative/|access-date=2019-12-25}}</ref> Although Trudeau initially spoke out against the idea of the bill in 2017, he did not take any actual action to prevent the bill from passing. During his election campaign in 2019, he avoided the topic as much as possible in order to maintain popularity in the polls within Quebec.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Zimonjic |first=Peter |date=December 13, 2021 |title=Trudeau says he won't step into Bill 21 debate to avoid triggering jurisdictional spat with Quebec |work=CBC News |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/trudeau-bill-21-jurisdiction-teacher-hijab-1.6283895}}</ref> The consensus among the 2019 candidates was that the bill was a provincial issue and they would not pursue action at a federal level if elected. Including NDP leader Jagmeet Singh who would personally be affected by the bill while in Quebec.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rabson |first=Mia |date=2019-10-08 |title=Singh's stance on Bill 21 called out by anti-hate group |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/politics/federal-election-2019/singh-s-stance-on-bill-21-called-out-by-anti-hate-group-1.4628795 |access-date=2023-10-20 |website=Federal Election 2019 |language=en}}{{dead link|date=July 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

During the [[2021 Canadian federal election|2021 federal election]], The English-language debate gained notoriety when the moderator posed a question to Blanchet that suggested some in English speaking Canada may view Quebec's [[Act respecting the laicity of the State|law on secularism]] as "discriminatory". He challenged her use of that word, and the response was seen as a turning point in the Bloc's campaign, which saw an upsurge in the polls after the debate.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Stevenson |first1=Verity |title=Controversial question in English debate may have galvanized Bloc voters |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/bloc-debate-reaction-1.6176663 |website=CBC News |access-date=September 26, 2021 |date=September 16, 2021 |archive-date=September 26, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210926213012/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/bloc-debate-reaction-1.6176663 |url-status=live }}</ref> The Quebec National Assembly passed a motion calling for a formal apology for the question.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/national/election-2021/national-assembly-calls-for-apology-for-english-debate-question | title=Quebec demands formal apology for controversial question at English debate }}</ref>

==Court challenges==
Since the law was first introduced in 2019, it has faced many legal challenges.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Montpetit|first=Jonathan|date=Dec 9, 2019|title=François Legault's high-stakes game with the courts and Quebec's secularism law|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/fran-ois-legault-s-high-stakes-game-with-the-courts-and-bill-21-1.5388695|website=CBC News}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Montpetit|first=Jonathan|date=December 12, 2019|title=One law, many challenges: How lawyers are trying to overturn Quebec's religious symbols ban|work=CBC News|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/bill-21-quebec-court-challenges-1.5393074|access-date=December 13, 2019}}</ref>

The [[National Council of Canadian Muslims]] (NCCM) and the [[Canadian Civil Liberties Association]] (CCLA) filed a legal challenge against the law which aimed to stay its application. The groups argue that the law is unconstitutional, irreparably harms religious minorities, and constitutes "state-sanctioned second-class citizenship".<ref>{{Cite web|date=June 18, 2019|title=Quebec Draws Challenge After Banning Many Public Workers From Wearing Religious Garb|url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/quebec-bill-21-lawsuit_n_5d08eed1e4b0f7b74426fb9a|website=HuffPost Canada}}</ref> The [[Quebec Court of Appeal]] later granted the petitioning organisations leave to appeal the claim for an injunction.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Small victory in court for groups fighting Bill 21|url=https://globalnews.ca/news/5714731/bill-21-superior-court-appeal/|website=Global News}}</ref> The Coalition Inclusion Quebec announced a challenge to the ruling at the Quebec Court of Appeal in order to strike down the entire law.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Group representing hijab-wearing teachers launches appeal against Bill 21 decision|url=https://globalnews.ca/news/7778250/group-hijab-wearing-teachers-launches-appeal-bill-21-decision/|website=Global News}}</ref> A 29-day hearing into challenges to the law was heard in the Quebec Superior Court in 2020.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Montpetit|first=Jonathan|date=December 21, 2020|title=As trial over Quebec religious symbols ban wraps up, minority rights hang in the balance|work=CBC|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/bill-21-laicity-democracy-1.5848103|access-date=April 3, 2021}}</ref>

In April 2021, Quebec Superior Court judge Marc-André Blanchard ruled that the law violated the [[freedom of expression]] and [[freedom of religion|religion]] of religious minorities (especially [[Islam in Canada|Muslim]] women).<ref name=cbc1/><ref name="Global News"/> Blanchard stated the law "in one way [violates] their freedom of religion, and in another, [does] the same in regards to their freedom of expression, since clothing constitutes both pure and simple expression, and also the manifestation of a religious belief."<ref>{{cite news|title=Quebec court upholds most of province's secularism law, exempts English school boards|url=https://www.winnipegfreepress.com/arts-and-life/life/faith/2021/04/20/quebec-judge-to-rule-today-on-challenge-to-quebecs-secularism-law-known-as-bill-21}}</ref> Nevertheless, he upheld most of the ban as the government had invoked the [[notwithstanding clause]]. However, he ruled that the provisions were unconstitutional, to the extent they applied to English-language school boards, as the notwithstanding clause cannot be used to restrict minority language rights protected by the ''Canadian Charter Rights and Freedoms''. Similarly, the notwithstanding clause cannot be used to restrict rights granted by [[Section 3 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms|Section 3 of the Canadian Charter]] to elected members of the legislative assemblies, so the law was unconstitutional to the extent it purported to apply to members of the National Assembly.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Perreaux|first=Les|date=2021-04-20|title=Quebec court upholds law banning religious dress, with exceptions for English schools, MNAs|language=en-CA|work=The Globe and Mail|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-quebec-court-upholds-law-banning-religious-dress-with-exceptions-for/|access-date=2021-12-16}}</ref>

On February 29 2024, The [[Quebec Court of Appeal]] ruled in favor of Quebec's Bill 21.<ref>[https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/quebec-appeal-court-decision-bill-21-1.7128447]</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://globalnews.ca/news/10325786/bill-21-quebec-appeals-court-ruling/ | title=Quebec Court of Appeal rules that secularism law known as Bill 21 is constitutional {{pipe}} Globalnews.ca }}</ref>

In 2025, the [[Supreme Court of Canada]] agreed to hear a challenge to the bill,<ref>{{Cite news |date=2025-01-23 |title=Supreme Court of Canada agrees to hear legal challenge to Quebec's secularism law |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-quebecs-controversial-secularism-law-to-be-tried-in-the-supreme-court/ |access-date=2025-10-08 |work=The Globe and Mail |language=en-CA}}</ref> with the court expected to rule on how provinces can invoke [[Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms|Section 33 of the ''Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms'']], the notwithstanding clause.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wherry |first=Aaron |date=2025-10-04 |title=What is the Supreme Court going to say about the notwithstanding clause? |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/supreme-court-notwithstanding-bill-21-analysis-1.7650639 |access-date=2025-10-08 |website=CBC}}</ref>
